claim: Thymus medulla epithelium establishes immune self-tolerance and comprises diverse cellular subsets.
source: Thymus medulla epithelium establishes immune self-tolerance and comprises diverse cellular subsets.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about thymus function.

claim: Functionally relevant medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) include a self-antigen-displaying subset that exhibits genome-wide promiscuous gene expression promoted by the nuclear protein Aire.
source: Functionally relevant medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) include a self-antigen-displaying subset that exhibits genome-wide promiscuous gene expression promoted by the nuclear protein Aire and that resembles a mosaic of extrathymic cells including mucosal tuft cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about Aire function in mTECs and is referenced in the introduction with citations (Derbinski et al., 2001; Anderson et al., 2002).

claim: Self-antigen-displaying mTECs resemble a mosaic of extrathymic cells including mucosal tuft cells.
source: Functionally relevant medullary thymic epithelial cells (mTECs) include a self-antigen-displaying subset that exhibits genome-wide promiscuous gene expression promoted by the nuclear protein Aire and that resembles a mosaic of extrathymic cells including mucosal tuft cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction (Farr et al., 2002; Michelson et al., 2022) describing cellular mimesis in mTEC subpopulations.

claim: An additional mTEC subset produces the chemokine CCL21, thereby attracting positively selected thymocytes from the cortex to the medulla.
source: An additional mTEC subset produces the chemokine CCL21, thereby attracting positively selected thymocytes from the cortex to the medulla.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction (Takahama et al., 2017; Ueno et al., 2004; Takahama, 2006).

claim: Both self-antigen-displaying and thymocyte-attracting mTEC subsets are essential for self-tolerance.
source: Both self-antigen-displaying and thymocyte-attracting mTEC subsets are essential for self-tolerance.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction (Kozai et al., 2017; Kurobe et al., 2006; Nitta et al., 2009) showing that loss of CCL21 or CCR7 leads to failure of self-tolerance.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs arise early during thymus ontogeny in mice.
source: We show that CCL21-expressing mTECs arise early during thymus ontogeny in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Self-antigen-displaying mTECs, including Aire-expressing mTECs and thymic tuft cells, are derived from CCL21-expressing cells.
source: Fate-mapping analysis reveals that self-antigen-displaying mTECs, including Aire-expressing mTECs and thymic tuft cells, are derived from CCL21-expressing cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fate-mapping experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The differentiation capability of CCL21-expressing embryonic mTECs is verified in reaggregate thymus experiments.
source: The differentiation capability of CCL21-expressing embryonic mTECs is verified in reaggregate thymus experiments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: CCL21-expressing embryonic mTECs carry a developmental potential to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs.
source: These results indicate that CCL21-expressing embryonic mTECs carry a developmental potential to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs, revealing that the sequential conversion of thymocyte-attracting subset into self-antigen-displaying subset serves to assemble functional diversity in the thymus medulla epithelium.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study, particularly from fate-mapping and reaggregate thymus experiments.

claim: The sequential conversion of thymocyte-attracting subset into self-antigen-displaying subset serves to assemble functional diversity in the thymus medulla epithelium.
source: These results indicate that CCL21-expressing embryonic mTECs carry a developmental potential to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs, revealing that the sequential conversion of thymocyte-attracting subset into self-antigen-displaying subset serves to assemble functional diversity in the thymus medulla epithelium.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion inferred from the experimental findings showing developmental conversion from CCL21-expressing to self-antigen-displaying mTECs.

claim: Promiscuous gene expression by a subpopulation of mTECs that express the nuclear protein Aire allows chromatin remodeling and genome-wide ectopic gene transcription.
source: Promiscuous gene expression by a subpopulation of mTECs that express the nuclear protein Aire allows chromatin remodeling and genome-wide ectopic gene transcription (Derbinski et al., 2001; Anderson et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Derbinski et al., 2001; Anderson et al., 2002).

claim: Cellular mimesis in other mTEC subpopulations relies on a mosaic of tissue-specific transcription factor-dependent cells that individually resemble specialized cell types, including mucosal tuft cells and microfold cells.
source: Cellular mimesis in other mTEC subpopulations relies on a mosaic of tissue-specific transcription factor-dependent cells that individually resemble specialized cell types, including mucosal tuft cells and microfold cells (Farr et al., 2002; Michelson et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Farr et al., 2002; Michelson et al., 2022).

claim: Positive selection-inducing TCR signals in newly generated cortical thymocytes elevate the expression of CCR7, a receptor for CCL21.
source: Positive selection-inducing TCR signals in newly generated cortical thymocytes elevate the expression of CCR7, a receptor for CCL21, and positively selected cortical thymocytes are therefore specifically attracted to migrate to the medullary region through the CCL21–CCR7-mediated chemotactic signals (Ueno et al., 2004; Takahama, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Ueno et al., 2004; Takahama, 2006).

claim: Two molecular species CCL21Ser and CCL21Leu with one amino acid difference are encoded in the mouse genome.
source: Two molecular species CCL21Ser and CCL21Leu with one amino acid difference are encoded in the mouse genome (Nakano and Gunn, 2001; Chen et al., 2002), and CCL21Ser encoded by Ccl21a locus is predominantly expressed in the thymus medulla (Kozai et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Nakano and Gunn, 2001; Chen et al., 2002; Kozai et al., 2017).

claim: CCL21Ser encoded by Ccl21a locus is predominantly expressed in the thymus medulla.
source: Two molecular species CCL21Ser and CCL21Leu with one amino acid difference are encoded in the mouse genome (Nakano and Gunn, 2001; Chen et al., 2002), and CCL21Ser encoded by Ccl21a locus is predominantly expressed in the thymus medulla (Kozai et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study (Kozai et al., 2017).

claim: In mice lacking either Ccr7 or Ccl21a, positively selected mature thymocytes fail to accumulate in the medulla, and therefore T cells fail to establish self-tolerance.
source: In mice lacking either Ccr7 or Ccl21a, positively selected mature thymocytes fail to accumulate in the medulla, and therefore T cells fail to establish self-tolerance (Kozai et al., 2017; Kurobe et al., 2006; Nitta et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Kozai et al., 2017; Kurobe et al., 2006; Nitta et al., 2009).

claim: Additional CCR7-ligand CCL19 has no appreciable role in the cortex-to-medulla migration of developing thymocytes.
source: Additional CCR7-ligand CCL19 has no appreciable role in the cortex-to-medulla migration of developing thymocytes (Kozai et al., 2017; Link et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Kozai et al., 2017; Link et al., 2007).

claim: Aire-expressing mTECs primarily belong to MHC-IIhigh CD80high mTEC subpopulation (mTEChigh).
source: Aire-expressing mTECs primarily belong to MHC-IIhigh CD80high mTEC subpopulation (mTEChigh) (Derbinski et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2006), whereas most thymic mimetic cells are detectable in MHC-IIlow CD80low mTEC subpopulation (mTEClow), which are derived from Aire-expressing mTEChigh cells (Michelson et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2018; Kadouri et al., 2020; Metzger et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Derbinski et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2006).

claim: Most thymic mimetic cells are detectable in MHC-IIlow CD80low mTEC subpopulation (mTEClow), which are derived from Aire-expressing mTEChigh cells.
source: Aire-expressing mTECs primarily belong to MHC-IIhigh CD80high mTEC subpopulation (mTEChigh) (Derbinski et al., 2005; Gray et al., 2006), whereas most thymic mimetic cells are detectable in MHC-IIlow CD80low mTEC subpopulation (mTEClow), which are derived from Aire-expressing mTEChigh cells (Michelson et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2018; Kadouri et al., 2020; Metzger et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Michelson et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2018; Kadouri et al., 2020; Metzger et al., 2013).

claim: The mTEClow subpopulation is heterogeneous and contains immature mTEC progenitors that differentiate into the Aire-expressing mTEChigh subpopulation.
source: The mTEClow subpopulation is heterogeneous and contains immature mTEC progenitors that differentiate into the Aire-expressing mTEChigh subpopulation (Rossi et al., 2007; Gäbler et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Rossi et al., 2007; Gäbler et al., 2007).

claim: The developmental progression of the self-antigen-displaying mTEC subset occurs in the following sequence: mTEClow progenitors -> mTEChigh Aire-expressing cells -> mTEClow mimetic cells.
source: Consequently, the developmental progression of the self-antigen-displaying mTEC subset is considered to occur in the following sequence: mTEClow progenitors -> mTEChigh Aire-expressing cells -> mTEClow mimetic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from previous studies cited in the introduction, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs are mostly included in the mTEClow subpopulation.
source: CCL21-expressing mTECs are mostly included in the mTEClow subpopulation (Lkhagvasuren et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study (Lkhagvasuren et al., 2013).

claim: In the postnatal thymus of 5-week-old Ccl21atdTomato/+ mice, CCL21-expressing cells were detected in keratin 14 (Krt14)-expressing medullary TECs.
source: In the postnatal thymus of 5-week-old Ccl21atdTomato/+ mice, CCL21-expressing cells were detected in keratin 14 (Krt14)-expressing medullary TECs (Figure 1A) and not in Ly51-expressing cortical TECs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CCL21-expressing cells in the postnatal thymus of 5-week-old Ccl21atdTomato/+ mice were not detected in Ly51-expressing cortical TECs.
source: In the postnatal thymus of 5-week-old Ccl21atdTomato/+ mice, CCL21-expressing cells were detected in keratin 14 (Krt14)-expressing medullary TECs (Figure 1A) and not in Ly51-expressing cortical TECs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ccl21atdTomato+ cells in the thymus are predominantly confined in EpCAM+Ly51−UEA1+ mTECs.
source: Flow cytometric analysis confirmed that Ccl21atdTomato+ cells in the thymus are predominantly confined in EpCAM+Ly51−UEA1+ mTECs (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Thymic medulla was abundant in CCL21 proteins.
source: In accordance with the medullary localization of CCL21-expressing mTECs, thymic medulla was abundant in CCL21 proteins (Figure 1E), which contribute to attracting CCR7-expressing positively selected thymocytes from the cortex (Takahama, 2006; Kozai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Most CCL21-expressing mTECs were distinct from Aire-expressing mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells.
source: Among mTECs, most CCL21-expressing mTECs were distinct from Aire-expressing mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs equally distributed throughout the medullary region and were enriched neither in the pericortical area, including the cortico-medullary junction area, nor in the central area within the medulla.
source: CCL21-expressing mTECs equally distributed throughout the medullary region and were enriched neither in the pericortical area, including the cortico-medullary junction area, nor in the central area within the medulla (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fluorescence distribution analysis shown in Figures 1G, 1H, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCL21-expressing cells in the central region of the thymus were prominent by embryonic day 15 (E15).
source: Analysis of embryonic thymus showed that CCL21-expressing cells in the central region of the thymus were prominent by embryonic day 15 (E15) (Figure 2A) and detectable as early as E13 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CCL21-expressing cells in the central region of the thymus were detectable as early as E13.
source: Analysis of embryonic thymus showed that CCL21-expressing cells in the central region of the thymus were prominent by embryonic day 15 (E15) (Figure 2A) and detectable as early as E13 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CCL21 proteins were detectable in the medullary region proximal to Ccl21atdTomato-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus by E15.
source: CCL21 proteins were detectable in the medullary region proximal to Ccl21atdTomato-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus by E15 (Figure 2D), indicating that Ccl21atdTomato-expressing E15 embryonic mTECs represent functionally relevant CCL21-expressing mTECs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Ccl21atdTomato-expressing E15 embryonic mTECs represent functionally relevant CCL21-expressing mTECs.
source: CCL21 proteins were detectable in the medullary region proximal to Ccl21atdTomato-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus by E15 (Figure 2D), indicating that Ccl21atdTomato-expressing E15 embryonic mTECs represent functionally relevant CCL21-expressing mTECs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the detection of CCL21 proteins in proximity to Ccl21atdTomato-expressing cells.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus were largely distinct from Aire-expressing mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells.
source: On the other hand, CCL21-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus were largely distinct from Aire-expressing mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus distributed throughout the medullary region and were not enriched in the pericortical areas including the cortico-medullary junctions.
source: Similar to the postnatal thymus, CCL21-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus distributed throughout the medullary region and were not enriched in the pericortical areas including the cortico-medullary junctions (Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fluorescence distribution analysis shown in Figures 2F, 2G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Ccl21a-Cre × CAG-loxP-EGFP mice, EGFP expression labeled cells that have transcribed Ccl21a previously and/or presently.
source: In Ccl21a-Cre × CAG-loxP-EGFP mice, EGFP expression labeled cells that have transcribed Ccl21a previously and/or presently (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for fate-mapping, based on the Cre-loxP system.

claim: In the postnatal thymus of 3-week-old Ccl21a-Cre × CAG-loxP-EGFP mice, EGFP signals in the thymus distributed prominently in the medullary region.
source: In the postnatal thymus of 3-week-old Ccl21a-Cre × CAG-loxP-EGFP mice, EGFP signals in the thymus distributed prominently in the medullary region (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: EGFP+ cells in the medulla were detected in Krt14+ mTECs, including Aire+ mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells.
source: EGFP+ cells in the medulla were detected in Krt14+ mTECs (Figure 3B), including Aire+ mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: EGFP+ cells in the thymus were detected exclusively in EpCAM+ CD45− TECs and not in EpCAM−CD45+ hematopoietic cells or EpCAM−CD45− cells.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of enzyme-digested thymus cells showed that EGFP+ cells in the thymus were detected exclusively in EpCAM+ CD45− TECs and not in EpCAM−CD45+ hematopoietic cells, including thymocytes and dendritic cells, or EpCAM−CD45− cells, including mesenchymal fibroblasts and endothelial cells (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Approximately 95% of UEA1+Ly51− mTECs were EGFP+, indicating that a vast majority of mTECs were derived from cells that previously transcribed Ccl21a.
source: Within EpCAM+CD45– TECs, approximately 95% of UEA1+Ly51− mTECs were EGFP+, indicating that a vast majority of mTECs were derived from cells that previously transcribed Ccl21a (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3F and 3G, with inference about developmental origin.

claim: Aire+UEA1+Ly51− cells and DCLK1+UEA1+Ly51−cells were detected in EpCAM+CD45− EGFP+ TECs.
source: Flow cytometric analysis also confirmed the detection of Aire+UEA1+Ly51− cells and DCLK1+UEA1+Ly51−cells in EpCAM+CD45− EGFP+ TECs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Self-antigen-displaying mTECs, including Aire+ mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells, which do not presently express CCL21, originate from Ccl21a+ progenitors.
source: Thus, self-antigen-displaying mTECs, including Aire+ mTECs and DCLK1+ thymic tuft cells, which do not presently express CCL21 (Figures 1F, 2E), originate from Ccl21a+ progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fate-mapping data showing EGFP+ Aire+ and DCLK1+ cells.

claim: Cre was detected specifically in the Ccl21a-expressing mTEClow subpopulation and not in the Psmb11-expressing cTECs or the Aire- and Tnfrsf11a-expressing mTEChigh subpopulation.
source: In the quantitative RT-PCR analysis of Cre, Ccl21a, and other TEC-associated genes, such as Aire, Tnfrsf11a, and Psmb11, Cre was detected specifically in the Ccl21a-expressing mTEClow subpopulation, which includes the majority of CCL21-expressing mTECs (Lkhagvasuren et al., 2013), and not in the Psmb11-expressing cTECs or the Aire- and Tnfrsf11a-expressing mTEChigh subpopulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Approximately two-thirds of postnatal cTECs are derived from cells that previously transcribed Ccl21a.
source: In addition to mTECs, approximately 66% of UEA1−Ly51+ cTECs in the postnatal thymus were EGFP+ in 3-week-old Ccl21a-Cre × CAG-loxP-EGFP mice (Figure 3F, G). Section analysis of the thymus verified the presence of EGFP+ cells in the cortex (Figure 3B). Because cTECs do not presently express Ccl21a transcripts (Kozai et al., 2017) (also shown in Figure 1B–D), these results indicate that approximately two-thirds of postnatal cTECs are derived from cells that previously transcribed Ccl21a (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data showing EGFP+ cTECs.

claim: EGFP+ and EGFP− cTECs showed high similarity in gene expression profiles among 20,230 genes detected.
source: The MA and volcano plots of RNA-sequencing data demonstrated high similarity in gene expression profiles between EGFP+ and EGFP− cTECs among 20,230 genes detected (Figure 4B, C), unlike the pronounced difference in global gene expression profiles between cTECs and mTECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Genes relevant for T cell-inducing and positive selection-inducing functions in cTECs were similarly abundant in EGFP+ and EGFP− cTECs.
source: The genes that are relevant for T cell-inducing and positive selection-inducing functions in cTECs, including Dll4, Il7, Cxcl12, Psmb11, Ctsl, Prss16, Cd83, H-2K, H-2D, and H2-Ab, were similarly abundant in EGFP+ and EGFP− cTECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: cTECs derived from cells that either do or do not transcribe Ccl21a are functionally comparable to promote the generation and positive selection of cortical thymocytes.
source: These results suggest that cTECs derived from cells that either do or do not transcribe Ccl21a are functionally comparable to promote the generation and positive selection of cortical thymocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the similar expression of functional genes in EGFP+ and EGFP− cTECs.

claim: Only 14 genes showed significantly higher expression in EGFP+ cTECs than in EGFP− cTECs.
source: Only 14 genes, including Ccl21a, showed significantly higher expression in EGFP+ cTECs than in EGFP− cTECs, whereas only one gene, the parathyroid hormone-encoding Pth, showed significantly lower expression in EGFP+ cTECs than in EGFP− cTECs (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: EGFP+ cTECs distributed unequally within the thymic cortex and were detected more frequently in the perimedullary cortical region than in the central cortical region or the subcapsular region of the cortex.
source: Interestingly, EGFP+ cTECs distributed unequally within the thymic cortex and were detected more frequently in the perimedullary cortical region than in the central cortical region or the subcapsular region of the cortex (Figure 4D, E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fluorescence distribution analysis shown in Figures 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Ly51+ total cTECs did not show unequal distribution in the thymic cortex.
source: In contrast, Ly51+ total cTECs did not show such an unequal distribution in the thymic cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by fluorescence distribution analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and 3C.

claim: The intrathymic proximity to the medullary region contributes to the previous expression of Ccl21a transcripts in cTECs.
source: Thus, the intrathymic proximity to the medullary region contributes to the previous expression of Ccl21a transcripts in cTECs, suggesting that approximately two-thirds of postnatal cTECs originate from Ccl21a+ cells generated in the thymic medulla.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the enrichment of EGFP+ cTECs in the perimedullary region.

claim: A vast majority of mTECs and approximately two-thirds of cTECs, particularly cTECs in the perimedullary cortical region, are derived from progenitor cells that previously transcribed Ccl21a.
source: Collectively, these fate-mapping experiments demonstrate that a vast majority of mTECs, including the self-antigen-displaying mTEC subset, and approximately two-thirds of cTECs, particularly cTECs in the perimedullary cortical region, are derived from progenitor cells that previously transcribed Ccl21a.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the fate-mapping experiments presented in the study.

claim: EGFP+ cells within Foxn1+ mTECs were detected in the central region of the thymus primordium in Ccl21a-Cre × CAG-loxP-EGFP mice as early as E11.
source: It is further interesting to note that EGFP+ cells within Foxn1+ mTECs were detected in the central region of the thymus primordium in Ccl21a-Cre × CAG-loxP-EGFP mice as early as E11 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The detection of EGFP+ cells occurred earlier in the ontogeny than the detection of Ccl21atdTomato+ mTECs by E13 and CCL21-protein-expressing mTECs by E15.
source: The detection of EGFP+ cells occurred earlier in the ontogeny than the detection of Ccl21atdTomato+ mTECs by E13 (Figure 2B) and CCL21-protein-expressing mTECs by E15 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a comparison of findings from different experiments showing temporal progression.

claim: Low-level Ccl21a transcription initiated as early as E11 during thymus organogenesis was sufficient to produce functional Cre proteins to mediate the expression of CAG-promoter-dependent EGFP proteins, but failed to produce a detectable amount of tdTomato or CCL21 proteins.
source: These sequential detections suggested that low-level Ccl21a transcription initiated as early as E11 during thymus organogenesis was sufficient to produce functional Cre proteins to mediate the expression of CAG-promoter-dependent EGFP proteins, but failed to produce a detectable amount of tdTomato or CCL21 proteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sequential detection of EGFP, tdTomato, and CCL21 proteins at different developmental stages.

claim: Ccl21a expression levels within individual Epcam+Foxn1+ TECs elevated during the embryogenesis from E12 to E14.
source: Indeed, single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of Ccl21a transcript counts demonstrated that Ccl21a expression levels within individual Epcam+Foxn1+ TECs elevated during the embryogenesis from E12 to E14 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At E14, Ccl21alow cells were detected at an equivalent frequency in β5t+ and β5t− TEC populations.
source: At E14, Ccl21alow cells were detected at an equivalent frequency in β5t+ and β5t− TEC populations (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ccl21a transcription in CCL21-expressing mTECs was further elevated from embryonic to postnatal development.
source: Ccl21a transcription in CCL21-expressing mTECs was further elevated from embryonic to postnatal development, as shown by single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of Ccl21a transcript counts (Figure 5B) and verified by flow cytometric analysis of Ccl21a-dependent tdTomato expression levels (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data (Figure 5B) and flow cytometry data (Figure 5C).

claim: Ccl21a+Foxn1+ mTECs detected during early thymus organogenesis were localized in the central region of the thymus primordium and were anatomically and transcriptomically distinguishable from Ccl21a+Gcm2+ parathyroid epithelial cells.
source: Importantly, Ccl21a+Foxn1+ mTECs detected during early thymus organogenesis were localized in the central region of the thymus primordium and were anatomically and transcriptomically distinguishable from Ccl21a+Gcm2+ parathyroid epithelial cells (Figures 2B and 5A, D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 2B, 5A) and single-cell RNA-sequencing data (Figure 5D).

claim: Ccl21a+ mTECs develop in the central region of the thymus primordium as early as E11 before the generation of detectably CCL21 protein-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus by E15.
source: These results reveal that Ccl21a+ mTECs develop in the central region of the thymus primordium as early as E11 before the generation of detectably CCL21 protein-expressing mTECs in the embryonic thymus by E15.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the temporal analysis of Ccl21a+ and CCL21+ mTECs during development.

claim: RANK-expressing mTEC-restricted progenitors arise in the thymus during embryogenesis downstream of mTEC stem cells, which originate from cTEC-trait-expressing bipotent progenitors.
source: Previous studies reported that embryonic thymus develops RANK-expressing mTEC-restricted progenitors, which have a developmental capability to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs, including Aire+ mTECs (Baik et al., 2016; Akiyama et al., 2016). RANK-expressing mTEC progenitors arise in the thymus during embryogenesis downstream of mTEC stem cells, which originate from cTEC-trait-expressing bipotent progenitors (Takahama et al., 2017; Baik et al., 2016; Akiyama et al., 2016; Sekai et al., 2014; Ohigashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Takahama et al., 2017; Baik et al., 2016; Akiyama et al., 2016; Sekai et al., 2014; Ohigashi et al., 2015).

claim: CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs were largely distinct cell populations within the embryonic thymus.
source: Interestingly, however, we found that CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs were largely distinct cell populations within the embryonic thymus (Figure 6A, B), although they were closely localized within the medullary region (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 6A) and flow cytometry data (Figure 6B).

claim: CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs were closely localized within the medullary region.
source: Interestingly, however, we found that CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs were largely distinct cell populations within the embryonic thymus (Figure 6A, B), although they were closely localized within the medullary region (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs were markedly different from RANK-expressing mTECs in global gene expression profiles.
source: RNA-sequencing analysis of CCL21+RANK- and CCL21−RANK+ TECs highly purified from Ccl21atdTomato Tnfrsf11a(RANK)Venus embryonic thymus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) demonstrated that CCL21-expressing mTECs were markedly different from RANK-expressing mTECs in global gene expression profiles (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs retained more cTEC-trait genes, including Psmb11, Cxcl12, Cd83, and Ackr4, than RANK-expressing mTECs.
source: Indeed, CCL21-expressing mTECs retained more cTEC-trait genes, including Psmb11, Cxcl12, Cd83, and Ackr4, than RANK-expressing mTECs (Figure 6E), suggesting that in comparison with RANK-expressing mTECs, CCL21-expressing mTECs are more recently derived from cTEC-trait-expressing bipotent TEC progenitors.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In comparison with RANK-expressing mTECs, CCL21-expressing mTECs are more recently derived from cTEC-trait-expressing bipotent TEC progenitors.
source: Indeed, CCL21-expressing mTECs retained more cTEC-trait genes, including Psmb11, Cxcl12, Cd83, and Ackr4, than RANK-expressing mTECs (Figure 6E), suggesting that in comparison with RANK-expressing mTECs, CCL21-expressing mTECs are more recently derived from cTEC-trait-expressing bipotent TEC progenitors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the retention of cTEC-trait genes in CCL21-expressing mTECs.

claim: Similar to RANK-expressing mTECs, CCL21-expressing mTECs expressed equivalent levels of some mTEC-trait transcripts, including Krt5 and Krt14.
source: However, similar to RANK-expressing mTECs, CCL21-expressing mTECs expressed equivalent levels of some mTEC-trait transcripts, including Krt5 and Krt14 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Trp63 and Pax1 were predominant in CCL21-expressing mTECs.
source: Among the genes associated with TEC progenitor activity (Senoo et al., 2007; Wallin et al., 1996; Ulyanchenko et al., 2016; Lucas et al., 2023; Hamazaki et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2014), Trp63 and Pax1 were predominant in CCL21-expressing mTECs, whereas Plet1, Krt19, Cldn3, Cldn4, and Ly6a were readily detectable in RANK-expressing mTECs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Plet1, Krt19, Cldn3, Cldn4, and Ly6a were readily detectable in RANK-expressing mTECs.
source: Among the genes associated with TEC progenitor activity (Senoo et al., 2007; Wallin et al., 1996; Ulyanchenko et al., 2016; Lucas et al., 2023; Hamazaki et al., 2007; Wong et al., 2014), Trp63 and Pax1 were predominant in CCL21-expressing mTECs, whereas Plet1, Krt19, Cldn3, Cldn4, and Ly6a were readily detectable in RANK-expressing mTECs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs in embryonic thymus are largely distinct from RANK-expressing mTECs, whereas CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs are proximally localized with each other within the thymus medulla.
source: Thus, CCL21-expressing mTECs in embryonic thymus are largely distinct from RANK-expressing mTECs, whereas CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs are proximally localized with each other within the thymus medulla.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the comparison of CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs.

claim: In mice deficient in CCL21, the accumulation of CD4+CD8- and CD4-CD8+ thymocytes in E17 thymic medullary region was defective.
source: Ccl21atdTomato+ mTECs had already become functional CCL21-protein-expressing mTECs by E17 (Figure 2), and the accumulation of CD4+CD8- and CD4-CD8+ thymocytes in E17 thymic medullary region was defective in mice deficient in CCL21 (Figure 7A–C), so that the reaggregate thymus experiments would address whether functionally relevant CCL21-expressing mTECs give rise to other mTEC subpopulations including Aire+ mTECs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7A-C.

claim: Ccl21atdTomato-positive EpCAM+CD45− mTECs isolated from Ccl21atdTomato/+ E17 embryos generated Aire+Krt14+ mTECs in the thymus reaggregated with RelB-deficient thymic stromal cells.
source: We found that Ccl21atdTomato-positive EpCAM+CD45− mTECs isolated from Ccl21atdTomato/+ E17 embryos generated Aire+Krt14+ mTECs in the thymus reaggregated with RelB-deficient thymic stromal cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data from reaggregate thymus experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Aire+Krt14+ mTECs also developed from an equal number of parallelly isolated Ccl21atdTomato-negative EpCAM+CD45− TECs.
source: Aire+Krt14+ mTECs also developed from an equal number of parallelly isolated Ccl21atdTomato-negative EpCAM+CD45− TECs (Figure 8B), which included cTEC–mTEC bipotent TEC progenitors (Takahama et al., 2017; Nusser et al., 2022)/.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data from reaggregate thymus experiments shown in Figure 8B.

claim: RelB-deficient thymic stromal reaggregates without additional TECs failed to generate Aire+Krt14+ mTECs.
source: RelB-deficient thymic stromal reaggregates without additional TECs failed to generate Aire+Krt14+ mTECs (Figure 8C), whereas control organ culture using RelB-heterozygous thymus apparently developed medullary regions that contained Aire+Krt14+ mTECs (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data from reaggregate thymus experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Control organ culture using RelB-heterozygous thymus apparently developed medullary regions that contained Aire+Krt14+ mTECs.
source: RelB-deficient thymic stromal reaggregates without additional TECs failed to generate Aire+Krt14+ mTECs (Figure 8C), whereas control organ culture using RelB-heterozygous thymus apparently developed medullary regions that contained Aire+Krt14+ mTECs (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data from reaggregate thymus experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Ccl21a+ mTECs have a developmental potential to give rise to Aire+Krt14+ mTECs, equivalently to and not statistically different from Ccl21a-negative TECs, including bipotent TEC progenitors.
source: Quantitative evaluation of Krt14+ medullary areas (Figure 8E) within total thymus aggregates (Figure 8F) demonstrated that Ccl21a+ mTECs have a developmental potential to give rise to Aire+Krt14+ mTECs, equivalently to and not statistically different from Ccl21a-negative TECs, including bipotent TEC progenitors (Figure 8G, H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative analysis of reaggregate thymus experiments shown in Figures 8E-H.

claim: Ccl21a+ mTECs were still detected in the Krt14+ medullary areas in reconstituted thymus reaggregated with either Ccl21a+ mTECs or Ccl21a-negative TECs.
source: Interestingly, Ccl21a+ mTECs were still detected in the Krt14+ medullary areas in reconstituted thymus reaggregated with either Ccl21a+ mTECs or Ccl21a-negative TECs (Figure 8I, J), indicating that Ccl21a+ mTECs have a potential to maintain themselves in the thymus and that Ccl21a-negative TECs have a developmental potential to produce Ccl21a+ mTECs.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data from reaggregate thymus experiments shown in Figures 8I and 8J.

claim: Ccl21a+ mTECs have a potential to maintain themselves in the thymus.
source: Interestingly, Ccl21a+ mTECs were still detected in the Krt14+ medullary areas in reconstituted thymus reaggregated with either Ccl21a+ mTECs or Ccl21a-negative TECs (Figure 8I, J), indicating that Ccl21a+ mTECs have a potential to maintain themselves in the thymus and that Ccl21a-negative TECs have a developmental potential to produce Ccl21a+ mTECs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the detection of Ccl21a+ mTECs in reconstituted thymus.

claim: Ccl21a-negative TECs have a developmental potential to produce Ccl21a+ mTECs.
source: Interestingly, Ccl21a+ mTECs were still detected in the Krt14+ medullary areas in reconstituted thymus reaggregated with either Ccl21a+ mTECs or Ccl21a-negative TECs (Figure 8I, J), indicating that Ccl21a+ mTECs have a potential to maintain themselves in the thymus and that Ccl21a-negative TECs have a developmental potential to produce Ccl21a+ mTECs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the detection of Ccl21a+ mTECs in reconstituted thymus reaggregated with Ccl21a-negative TECs.

claim: Functionally relevant CCL21-expressing mTECs have a developmental potential to give rise to Aire-expressing mTECs.
source: Most importantly, these results directly indicate that functionally relevant CCL21-expressing mTECs have a developmental potential to give rise to Aire-expressing mTECs.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion drawn from the reaggregate thymus experiments.

claim: Ccl21atdTomato-positive EpCAM+CD45− mTECs isolated from 4-week-old Ccl21atdTomato/+ mice did not exhibit any signs of Aire+Krt14+ mTEC generation in the thymus reaggregated with RelB-deficient thymic stromal cells.
source: In contrast to CCL21-expressing mTECs isolated from E17 embryos, Ccl21atdTomato-positive EpCAM+CD45− mTECs isolated from 4-week-old Ccl21atdTomato/+ mice did not exhibit any signs of Aire+Krt14+ mTEC generation in the thymus reaggregated with RelB-deficient thymic stromal cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–G), suggesting a decline in the developmental potential of CCL21+ mTECs during the ontogeny from embryonic to postnatal period.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data from reaggregate thymus experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-G.

claim: There is a decline in the developmental potential of CCL21+ mTECs during the ontogeny from embryonic to postnatal period.
source: In contrast to CCL21-expressing mTECs isolated from E17 embryos, Ccl21atdTomato-positive EpCAM+CD45− mTECs isolated from 4-week-old Ccl21atdTomato/+ mice did not exhibit any signs of Aire+Krt14+ mTEC generation in the thymus reaggregated with RelB-deficient thymic stromal cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–G), suggesting a decline in the developmental potential of CCL21+ mTECs during the ontogeny from embryonic to postnatal period.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of Aire+ mTEC generation from postnatal CCL21+ mTECs in reaggregate experiments.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs were localized specifically in the central region of the thymus and were Krt14+ throughout development including E17 embryos.
source: Throughout the development including E17 embryos, CCL21-expressing mTECs were localized specifically in the central region of the thymus and were Krt14+ (Figures 1, 2, 6,, 9A).
evidence: This is a summary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The global gene expression profiles were largely different between embryonic Ccl21alow mTECs and 4-week-old postnatal Ccl21ahigh mTECs.
source: However, single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis demonstrated that the global gene expression profiles were largely different between embryonic Ccl21alow mTECs and 4-week-old postnatal Ccl21ahigh mTECs (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The majority of CCL21-expressing mTECs at E17 but not the postnatal period simultaneously expressed cTEC-associated protein Ly51 and mTEC-associated UEA1-binding molecules on the cell surface.
source: Indeed, the majority of CCL21-expressing mTECs at E17 but not the postnatal period simultaneously expressed cTEC-associated protein Ly51 and mTEC-associated UEA1-binding molecules on the cell surface (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Ly51 expression was lower in embryonic TECs than postnatal TECs.
source: Ly51 expression was lower in embryonic TECs than postnatal TECs (Ripen et al., 2011) and equivalently distributed in the thymus including the medullary region defined by Krt14-expressing mTECs centrally localized in E17 thymus (Figure 9A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study (Ripen et al., 2011) and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: There is a difference in molecular expression profiles, including Ly51 expression, between E17 CCL21- and postnatal CCL21-expressing mTECs.
source: These results highlight the difference in molecular expression profiles, including Ly51 expression, between E17 CCL21- and postnatal CCL21-expressing mTECs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of embryonic and postnatal CCL21-expressing mTECs.

claim: Functional conversion of the thymocyte-attracting mTEC subset into the self-antigen-displaying mTEC subset offers an interesting implication that the thymus medulla is formed by initially generating CCL21-expressing mTECs and attracting CCR7-expressing positively selected thymocytes from the cortex even before the subsequent display of self-antigens mediated by Aire+ mTECs and thymic mimetic cells.
source: Functional conversion of the thymocyte-attracting mTEC subset into the self-antigen-displaying mTEC subset offers an interesting implication that the thymus medulla is formed by initially generating CCL21-expressing mTECs and attracting CCR7-expressing positively selected thymocytes from the cortex even before the subsequent display of self-antigens mediated by Aire+ mTECs and thymic mimetic cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings regarding the developmental sequence of mTEC subsets.

claim: Failure to establish self-tolerance by the loss of Ccr7 or Ccl21a in the thymus underscored the importance of functional CCL21-expressing mTEC subset.
source: Failure to establish self-tolerance by the loss of Ccr7 or Ccl21a in the thymus (Kozai et al., 2017; Kurobe et al., 2006; Nitta et al., 2009) underscored the importance of functional CCL21-expressing mTEC subset.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (Kozai et al., 2017; Kurobe et al., 2006; Nitta et al., 2009).

claim: The present results showing developmental potential of functional CCL21-expressing mTECs to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs reveals an additionally important function of CCL21-expressing mTECs in forming the diversity in thymus medulla epithelium, including the self-antigen-displaying mTEC subset.
source: Our present results showing developmental potential of functional CCL21-expressing mTECs to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs reveals an additionally important function of CCL21-expressing mTECs in forming the diversity in thymus medulla epithelium, including the self-antigen-displaying mTEC subset.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings of the study.

claim: Stepwise progression in mTEC development from thymocyte-attracting function to self-antigen-displaying function fits stepwise requirement to initially recruit newly generated T cells from the thymic cortex before tolerizing T cells to self-antigens.
source: Stepwise progression in mTEC development from thymocyte-attracting function to self-antigen-displaying function fits stepwise requirement to initially recruit newly generated T cells from the thymic cortex before tolerizing T cells to self-antigens.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the developmental progression.

claim: Down-regulation of CCL21 in functionally converted self-antigen-displaying mTECs may further contribute to the prevention of excessive negative selection of newly generated T cells to self-antigens.
source: Down-regulation of CCL21 in functionally converted self-antigen-displaying mTECs may further contribute to the prevention of excessive negative selection of newly generated T cells to self-antigens.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of CCL21 down-regulation.

claim: The function of the thymus medulla is not limited to the establishment of self-tolerance in conventional αβ T cells but extends to the development of innate lymphocytes, including invariant NKT cells and γδ T cells.
source: Recent studies demonstrated that the function of the thymus medulla is not limited to the establishment of self-tolerance in conventional αβ T cells but extends to the development of innate lymphocytes, including invariant NKT cells and γδ T cells (White et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies (White et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2012).

claim: The developmental capability of CCL21-expressing mTECs may further extend to additional mTEC subpopulations that contribute to supporting the development of innate invariant lymphocytes.
source: The developmental capability of CCL21-expressing mTECs may further extend to additional mTEC subpopulations that contribute to supporting the development of innate invariant lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other mTEC subpopulations.

claim: CCL21-expressing mTECs may represent a primordial mTECs which separate newly generated αβ T cells, γδ T cells, and NKT cells from the thymic cortex to the medullary microenvironment for further selection and maturation.
source: Thus, CCL21-expressing mTECs may represent a primordial mTECs which separate newly generated αβ T cells, γδ T cells, and NKT cells from the thymic cortex to the medullary microenvironment for further selection and maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the role of CCL21-expressing mTECs.

claim: The ability to give rise to Aire+ mTECs was not detectable in postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.
source: In contrast to the robust generation of Aire+ mTECs from embryonic CCL21+ mTECs, our results show that the ability to give rise to Aire+ mTECs was not detectable in postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from reaggregate thymus experiments comparing embryonic and postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.

claim: The fact that no Aire+ mTECs were detected in reaggregate thymus organ culture may reflect a postnatal decline in the developmental potential of CCL21+ mTECs.
source: The fact that no Aire+ mTECs were detected in reaggregate thymus organ culture may reflect a postnatal decline in the developmental potential of CCL21+ mTECs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lack of Aire+ mTEC generation from postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.

claim: It is possible that the developmental kinetics and the requirements for postnatal CCL21+ mTECs may be different from those for E17 CCL21+ mTECs, so that the reaggregate thymus organ culture conditions for detecting the development of E17 CCL21+ mTECs may not be optimal for the detection of the survival and development of postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.
source: However, it is also possible that the developmental kinetics and the requirements for postnatal CCL21+ mTECs may be different from those for E17 CCL21+ mTECs, so that the reaggregate thymus organ culture conditions for detecting the development of E17 CCL21+ mTECs may not be optimal for the detection of the survival and development of postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the lack of Aire+ mTEC generation from postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.

claim: CCL21+ mTECs may be heterogenous in developmental capability.
source: We think that CCL21+ mTECs may be heterogenous in developmental capability.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the heterogeneity in CCL21+ mTECs.

claim: Embryonic CCL21+ mTECs, which give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs including Aire+ mTECs and mimetic mTECs, may also terminally differentiate into a subpopulation of CCL21+ mTECs, which no longer have further developmental potential, and which represent the majority of postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.
source: Embryonic CCL21+ mTECs, which give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs including Aire+ mTECs and mimetic mTECs, may also terminally differentiate into a subpopulation of CCL21+ mTECs, which no longer have further developmental potential, and which represent the majority of postnatal CCL21+ mTECs.
evidence: This is a speculative model for the heterogeneity and developmental potential of CCL21+ mTECs.

claim: Developmental capability to become cTECs is shown in Ccl21a gene-expressing cells.
source: Developmental capability to become cTECs is shown in Ccl21a gene-expressing cells, and it is unknown whether CCL21-protein-expressing functional mTECs retain the developmental potential to give rise to cTECs.
evidence: This is a statement about the findings regarding cTEC development from Ccl21a-expressing cells.

claim: It is unknown whether CCL21-protein-expressing functional mTECs retain the developmental potential to give rise to cTECs.
source: Developmental capability to become cTECs is shown in Ccl21a gene-expressing cells, and it is unknown whether CCL21-protein-expressing functional mTECs retain the developmental potential to give rise to cTECs.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the current findings.

claim: At least a fraction of Ccl21a transcript-expressing mTECs retain a bipotent developmental potential to give rise to both cTECs and mTECs.
source: Consequently, we think that at least a fraction of Ccl21a transcript-expressing mTECs retain a bipotent developmental potential to give rise to both cTECs and mTECs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fate-mapping data showing cTEC and mTEC development from Ccl21a-expressing cells.

claim: It is unclear whether most Ccl21a-expressing mTECs retain a bipotent developmental potential for cTECs and mTECs or Ccl21a-expressing mTECs represent a mixture of bipotent progenitors and lineage-committed mTEC progenitors.
source: It is unclear whether most Ccl21a-expressing mTECs retain a bipotent developmental potential for cTECs and mTECs or Ccl21a-expressing mTECs represent a mixture of bipotent progenitors and lineage-committed mTEC progenitors.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the heterogeneity of Ccl21a-expressing mTECs.

claim: Initial signals to promote bipotent progenitors to mTEC lineage may be provided by molecules restricted in the central region of the embryonic thymus.
source: Because of the unequal distribution of EGFP-labeled cTECs within the thymic cortex, initial signals to promote bipotent progenitors to mTEC lineage may be provided by molecules restricted in the central region of the embryonic thymus, and those signals may promote the transcription of Ccl21a at an early stage of mTECs, which still retain the potential to become cTECs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the unequal distribution of EGFP+ cTECs.

claim: CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs are proximally localized within the medullary region in the thymus.
source: CCL21- and RANK-expressing mTECs are detectable in E13 embryonic thymus, are proximally localized within the medullary region in the thymus, and are capable of generating Aire-expressing mTECs.

source: Our results show that 95% of mTECs are labeled with EGFP fluorescence and therefore derived from Ccl21a+progenitors, whereas 5% of mTECs are not labeled with EGFP fluorescence in Ccl21a-Cre × loxP-EGFP mice.

source: Our previous study using β5t-driven Cre mice indicated fate-mapping of 95% EGFP+ mTECs in CAG-loxP-stop-loxP-EGFP-transgenic reporter mice used in this study and >99.5% ZsGreen+ mTECs in Rosa26-loxP-ZsGreen-knock-in reporter mice (Ohigashi et al., 2013).

source: A previous study detected Ccl21a transcripts within a podoplanin-expressing TEC subpopulation that resembled immature TECs in postnatal thymus (Onder et al., 2015).

source: In conclusion, the present study establishes that CCL21-expressing functional mTEC subset carries a developmental potential to give rise to self-antigen-displaying mTECs, revealing that the sequential conversion of functionally distinct mTEC subsets from thymocyte-attracting cells into self-antigen-displaying cells contributes to the functional diversification of thymus medulla epithelium during embryonic development.

claim: The sequential conversion of functionally distinct mTEC subsets from thymocyte-attracting cells into self-antigen-displaying cells contributes to the functional diversification of thymus medulla epithelium during embryonic development.
